questions.q: What distinguishes Rx(θ), Ry(θ), and Rz(θ) from the fixed gates X, Y, Z, H, S, and T?
options: Rotation gates are not unitary
Rotation gates have a continuous, adjustable angle parameter θ, while the fixed gates have no adjustable parameter at all
Rotation gates only apply to multi-qubit states
Rotation gates cannot be represented as 2x2 matrices
questions.explain: Every fixed gate in this chapter (X, Y, Z, H, S, T) has one specific matrix. Rx, Ry, and Rz are entire families parameterized by θ, giving access to a continuum of single-qubit unitaries — the fixed gates turn out to be special cases at specific angles.

questions.q: Direct computation shows Ry(π/2)|0⟩ equals (0.7071, 0.7071), numerically identical to H|0⟩. What does computing Ry(π/2)|1⟩ reveal?
options: It also exactly matches H|1⟩, proving Ry(π/2) = H
It equals (-0.7071, 0.7071), the negative of H|1⟩ — showing the two gates agree on one basis vector but not the other
It equals (0, 0), showing Ry(π/2) destroys the state
It cannot be computed without complex numbers
questions.explain: Ry(π/2)|1⟩ computes to (-sin(π/4), cos(π/4)) = (-0.7071, 0.7071), while H|1⟩ = (0.7071, -0.7071) — entry-by-entry negatives of each other. This proves that matching one basis vector's output is not sufficient to conclude two gates are identical; both basis vectors (the full matrix) must be checked.

questions.q: Computing Rx(π) directly gives the matrix [[0,-i],[-i,0]], which equals -i times the X matrix [[0,1],[1,0]]. What does this relationship mean?
options: Rx(π) and X are completely unrelated gates
Rx(π) and X are identical matrices with no differences
Rx(π) equals X up to a global phase factor of -i, making them physically indistinguishable by measurement despite having different matrix entries
Rx(π) is not a valid unitary matrix
questions.explain: A global phase factor like -i multiplies every entry of the matrix (and therefore every amplitude of any output state) by the same constant. Since |−i|²=1, this never changes measurement probabilities, so Rx(π) and X produce identical measurement statistics in any circuit even though their matrix entries differ by that constant factor.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a 'global phase' and a 'relative phase,' as used in this lesson and the Pauli-gates lesson?
options: There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
A global phase multiplies the entire state vector uniformly and is never measurable; a relative phase changes one amplitude's angle relative to another and can become observable through interference
A global phase only applies to two-qubit systems
A relative phase always changes measurement probabilities immediately, with no further gates needed
questions.explain: Global phase (e.g. the -i in Rx(π) = -i·X) multiplies every amplitude by the same factor, so it cancels out of every |amplitude|² calculation and is undetectable. Relative phase (e.g. the sign difference Z introduces on |1⟩, or between Ry(π/2)|1⟩ and H|1⟩) only shows up between amplitudes and can be converted into a measurable probability difference by a later interference-producing gate like H.

questions.q: Why do Rx, Ry, and Rz matter for real quantum hardware, beyond being a mathematical generalization?
options: They don't — real hardware only implements the fixed gates directly

Because physical qubit control (e.g. a microwave or laser pulse's duration and detuning) directly sets a continuous angle θ, making rotation gates the natural match for how hardware actually drives a qubit
Because rotation gates are the only gates that preserve normalization
Because rotation gates eliminate the need for measurement entirely
questions.explain: Superconducting qubits, trapped ions, and other real hardware platforms are controlled by pulses whose parameters set a rotation angle directly, so Rx(θ), Ry(θ), Rz(θ) map naturally onto physical control knobs. This is why rotation gates become central once the course moves into hardware-level and variational circuit design.
